To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
individual investors tend to buy stocks that they have first noticed, e.g., because they have been mentioned in the news, or because they have had large price movements.

individual investors are more likely to buy stocks that are in the news, have high trading volume, and have extreme one-day returns, and that institutional investors are not more likely to buy these stocks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the attention of individual and institutional investors affects the prices of stocks.
the role of attention in the stock market.

the effects that attention has on the trading decisions of investors, and we show that attention can affect the buying decisions of individual investors but not the selling decisions of individual or institutional investors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stock market is not efficient.
the stock market is a market for attention and not a market for securities.
the stock market is a place of risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we find that investors buy stocks in the news and that they do so in part because they are not aware of the full set of stocks that are available for purchase.
investors buy what they see, and they see what is in the news.
the market is not efficient, but it is rational.
The main takeaway from our work is that
individual investors buy more stocks that have recently caught their attention.
individual investors tend to buy stocks that are in the news and that they tend to sell stocks that are out of the news.
individual investors tend to buy attention-grabbing securities, while institutional investors tend to sell attention-grabbing (and, hence, popular) securities.
